etymology: English personal name. John (Hebrew Yochanan, "Yahweh is gracious"); Gill, an English surname. John Gill (1697-1771) was a Particular Baptist pastor, Hebraist, and systematic theologian of London.
biblical_def: John Gill (1697-1771) was the great Particular Baptist scholar-pastor of the 18th century — a self-taught Hebraist of formidable learning, the first Baptist to write a complete systematic theology and a complete verse-by-verse commentary on the whole Bible, and the predecessor (three pastorates removed) of Charles Spurgeon at the Southwark congregation. Gill pastored the same London church for over fifty years. His Exposition of the Old and New Testaments (the "Gill's Commentary," nine folio volumes) and his Body of Doctrinal and Practical Divinity were monuments of Particular Baptist scholarship, saturated with rabbinic and patristic learning. Theologically he was a high Calvinist — so high that later generations debated whether his refusal to issue indiscriminate gospel "offers" tipped into the hyper-Calvinist denial of the free offer (the dictionary's hyper-calvinism entry marks the line). Gill himself preached the gospel and called sinners to Christ, but his system's reluctance about the universal offer became a point of controversy that Andrew Fuller would later answer. Spurgeon, who inherited Gill's pulpit lineage and esteemed his commentary, nonetheless gently distanced himself from Gill's hyper-Calvinist tendencies while honoring his learning. Gill stands as the towering Baptist scholar of his century: confessional, immensely learned, and a defender of the doctrines of grace in an age of rising Arminianism.

corruption_summary: John Gill is corrupted when his immense learning is forgotten, when his high Calvinism is either dismissed wholesale as hyper-Calvinism or defended uncritically, or when the genuine controversy over the free offer that surrounded his system is airbrushed away.
corruption_paragraphs: Hyper-Calvinist over-simplification. Gill is frequently labeled, flatly, a hyper-Calvinist — as though he denied that the gospel should be preached to all. The reality is more careful: Gill preached Christ and called sinners, but his theological system was reluctant about the well-meant universal offer in a way that fed the hyper-Calvinism of some of his followers. The dictionary distinguishes Gill's actual position from both the caricature (he was not a non-evangelistic recluse) and the uncritical defense (his system did have a real weakness on the free offer that Andrew Fuller rightly addressed). Honor the scholar; mark the genuine point of controversy.

Learning-forgotten misreading. Gill's nine-volume commentary and his systematic theology represent a depth of rabbinic, patristic, and linguistic learning rare in any age and astonishing in a self-taught man. Modern Baptists who know him only as a name, or only as "the hyper-Calvinist," have forgotten the towering scholar who gave the Particular Baptists their first complete systematic theology and whole-Bible exposition. He is a standing rebuke to the anti-intellectualism that has sometimes marked later Baptist life.

etymology: English personal name. Andrew (Greek Andreas, "manly"); Fuller, an English occupational surname (a fuller of cloth). Andrew Fuller (1754-1815) was a Particular Baptist pastor, theologian, and the doctrinal architect of the modern missionary movement.
biblical_def: Andrew Fuller (1754-1815) was the Particular Baptist theologian whose recovery of the free offer of the gospel within a fully Calvinistic framework broke the grip of hyper-Calvinism on the English Baptists and laid the doctrinal foundation for the modern missionary movement. Largely self-educated, Fuller pastored at Soham and then for thirty-three years at Kettering. His landmark work, The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785), argued that the gospel is to be offered freely to all without distinction, that all who hear are duty-bound to believe ("duty-faith"), and that the universal offer is fully compatible with particular election and definite atonement. This "Fullerism" answered the hyper-Calvinism that had paralyzed Baptist evangelism — the notion that since only the elect would believe, the gospel need not be pressed on all. Fuller's theology directly enabled the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society (1792), of which he became the first secretary, holding the rope while his friend William Carey went down into the missionary well in India. Fuller also wrote major polemical works against Socinianism, Deism, and Sandemanianism. He is the indispensable bridge between the high Calvinism of Gill and the missionary fervor of Carey: the man who showed that the doctrines of grace, rightly held, fuel rather than freeze the proclamation of the gospel to all the world.

corruption_summary: Andrew Fuller is corrupted when "Fullerism" is caricatured as a softening of Calvinism toward Arminianism, when his recovery of the free offer is forgotten by modern hyper-Calvinists, or when his missionary catalytic role is severed from the Calvinistic theology that drove it.
corruption_paragraphs: Crypto-Arminian caricature. Hyper-Calvinist critics have charged that Fuller's free offer and duty-faith smuggled Arminianism into the Baptist tradition. The charge fails: Fuller held unconditional election, definite atonement, and effectual calling without compromise; his contribution was to show that these doctrines REQUIRE rather than forbid the universal offer, because the warrant for faith is the command and promise of the gospel, not the hearer's secret election. Fuller out-argued both the Arminians and the hyper-Calvinists from within consistent Calvinism. To call him crypto-Arminian is to miss the precise thing he accomplished.

Missions-severed-from-doctrine misreading. Modern accounts sometimes celebrate Fuller as a missions pioneer while treating his Calvinism as incidental baggage. The history runs the other way: it was precisely Fuller's recovery of the free offer WITHIN Calvinism that made the Baptist Missionary Society theologically possible. Carey could go to India because Fuller had shown that the doctrines of grace command, rather than excuse, the proclamation of the gospel to all nations. The missions movement was born from the doctrine, not in spite of it.

etymology: English personal name. William (Germanic, "resolute protector"); Carey, an English surname. William Carey (1761-1834) was a Particular Baptist missionary to India, called the "father of modern missions."
biblical_def: William Carey (1761-1834) was the Particular Baptist cobbler-turned-missionary whose vision and labor made him the father of the modern Protestant missionary movement. A self-educated shoemaker who taught himself Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and several other languages while mending shoes, Carey was gripped by the unreached nations and wrote his epoch-making An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792), which demolished the hyper-Calvinist objection that the Great Commission was binding only on the apostles. His famous sermon on Isaiah 54:2-3 issued the watchword of the movement: "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God." That year, with Andrew Fuller and others, he founded the Baptist Missionary Society and sailed for India in 1793. He spent forty-one years there without a furlough, settling at Serampore, where he and his colleagues (the "Serampore Trio" with Joshua Marshman and William Ward) translated the Scriptures, in whole or part, into dozens of Indian languages and dialects, established schools and a college, fought the practice of widow-burning (sati), and labored against caste injustice. Carey buried a son and watched his first wife descend into mental illness; he pressed on. His combination of definite-atonement Calvinism, linguistic genius, and dogged perseverance set the pattern for two centuries of Protestant missions. The doctrines of grace did not freeze his zeal; they fueled it.

corruption_summary: William Carey is corrupted when reduced to a motivational slogan, when his missionary labor is severed from his Calvinistic theology, or when modern missiology claims his name while abandoning the gospel of definite atonement and conversion that drove him.
corruption_paragraphs: Slogan-reduction. Carey is widely known for one sentence — "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God" — lifted from its sermon and printed on conference banners. The slogan is true, but the man behind it was a definite-atonement Calvinist, a translator of staggering discipline, and a sufferer who buried a child and bore a wife's madness across decades in a foreign land. To keep the slogan and lose the theology, the discipline, and the suffering is to keep the poster and lose the missionary.

Gospel-severed missiology. Modern missiology sometimes invokes Carey's name while redefining the missionary task away from conversion and toward social transformation, interfaith dialogue, or development work alone. Carey did fight sati and caste injustice — but as the overflow of a gospel that called individual sinners to repentance and faith in Christ, and that drove him to translate the Scriptures so that they could read the call for themselves. His social reform flowed from gospel conversion; it did not replace it. The dictionary honors the whole Carey: the converting gospel first, the social fruit following.

etymology: English personal name. Thomas (Aramaic, "twin"); Manton, an English surname. Thomas Manton (1620-1677) was an English Puritan preacher and a clerk of the Westminster Assembly.
biblical_def: Thomas Manton (1620-1677) was one of the great Puritan expository preachers, a clerk of the Westminster Assembly, and the author of vast bodies of sermon-commentary that Spurgeon and the Banner of Truth would later prize. Educated at Oxford, Manton ministered in Stoke Newington and then at St. Paul's, Covent Garden, in London. He was chosen as one of the clerks of the Westminster Assembly and was esteemed among the moderate Presbyterian Puritans. At the Restoration in 1660 he was offered the deanery of Rochester but, with some two thousand other ministers, was ejected from the Church of England by the Act of Uniformity (1662) for refusing to conform — one of the great body of ejected Puritans whose Nonconformity shaped English Dissent. Manton's enduring legacy is his preaching: his complete works run to twenty-two volumes, dominated by massive expository series, most famously his commentaries on James, Jude, and the 119th Psalm (the last running to 190 sermons). His preaching is plain, doctrinally rich, searching, and pastorally warm in the best Puritan manner. J.C. Ryle wrote the biographical introduction to Manton's collected works and ranked him among the soundest of the Puritan divines. Manton models the Puritan expository ideal: the patient, sequential, doctrinally-full preaching of the biblical text, applied searchingly to the conscience.

corruption_summary: Thomas Manton is corrupted when his vast expository labor is dismissed as outdated Puritan verbosity, when his ejection is read as mere ecclesiastical politics rather than conscience-bound Nonconformity, or when the searching application that marks his preaching is lost in favor of mere information.
corruption_paragraphs: Verbosity dismissal. Twenty-two volumes, 190 sermons on a single psalm — modern readers, formed by brevity, may dismiss Manton's output as the long-windedness of a bygone age. The Puritan expository method was not padding but patience: the slow, sequential, doctrinally-full opening of the text, with searching application to the conscience at every turn. Manton's 190 sermons on Psalm 119 are not 190 ways of saying the same thing; they are 190 patient meditations that mine a single psalm for the whole of the Christian life. The reward of reading him is the reward of all the Puritans: depth that brevity cannot give.

Politics-not-conscience misreading. Manton's ejection in 1662, with some two thousand fellow ministers, is sometimes read as a casualty of Restoration church politics. For Manton it was a matter of conscience bound to Scripture: he would not subscribe what he could not affirm before God. The Great Ejection produced English Nonconformity and cost its ministers their livings, their pulpits, and often their liberty. Manton chose the loss rather than violate his conscience. The dictionary honors the conscience, not merely the historical event.

etymology: English personal name. Thomas (Aramaic, "twin"); Brooks, an English surname. Thomas Brooks (1608-1680) was an English Puritan preacher and devotional writer known for his vivid, aphoristic style.
biblical_def: Thomas Brooks (1608-1680) was an English Puritan preacher and devotional author whose vivid, image-rich, and intensely practical writing made him one of the most quotable of all the Puritans. Educated at Cambridge, Brooks ministered in London, including at St. Margaret's, Fish Street, and was among the ministers ejected in 1662 for Nonconformity. He continued to preach during the dark years of plague and fire that struck London in the 1660s, ministering when many fled. Brooks's most famous work, Precious Remedies against Satan's Devices (1652), is a classic of spiritual warfare: it catalogs the devil's stratagems for drawing the soul into sin and despair, and sets against each one the biblical remedy. His other devotional works — The Mute Christian under the Smarting Rod (on submission in affliction), Heaven on Earth (on assurance), The Unsearchable Riches of Christ, and Apples of Gold — are beloved for their warmth, their dense biblical allusion, and their memorable turns of phrase. Brooks wrote, famously, that "a humble heart is the habitation of the Trinity" and that affliction is the diamond dust heaven polishes its jewels with. His style is the Puritan plain method warmed by a poet's instinct for the apt image. He represents the experiential, devotional wing of Puritanism — the application of sound doctrine to the inner life of the believer with searching tenderness.

corruption_summary: Thomas Brooks is corrupted when his quotable aphorisms are stripped from their doctrinal substance and circulated as decorative spirituality, when his teaching on Satan's devices is dismissed as superstition, or when his experiential warmth is mistaken for the modern therapeutic register it preceded and opposed.
corruption_paragraphs: Aphorism-stripping. Brooks is among the most quoted Puritans on social media — his vivid one-liners about humility, affliction, and the riches of Christ circulate widely. But the aphorisms were forged within dense, doctrinally-grounded, Scripture-saturated treatises; lifted out and prettified, they become decorative spirituality detached from the searching theology that gave them force. "A humble heart is the habitation of the Trinity" is a true and beautiful line, but in Brooks it sits within pages of biblical argument about the nature of humility and the indwelling God. Read the treatise, not just the quote.

Therapeutic-confusion. Brooks's warmth, his attention to the inner life, and his tenderness toward the afflicted soul can be mistaken for the modern therapeutic register — as though he were an early self-help writer. He was the opposite. His experiential Puritanism applied hard doctrine (sin, Satan, sovereignty, the cross, eternity) to the inner life with searching realism; he comforted the afflicted by directing them to God's sovereign purposes in their suffering, not by affirming their feelings. His "Mute Christian under the Smarting Rod" teaches submission to God's chastening hand, not the self-validation the therapeutic age would later substitute.

etymology: Scottish personal name. Thomas (Aramaic, "twin"); Boston, a surname. Thomas Boston (1676-1732) was a Scottish Presbyterian pastor and theologian of the Marrow tradition.
biblical_def: Thomas Boston (1676-1732) was a Scottish Presbyterian pastor and theologian whose experiential, free-grace preaching and his role in the Marrow Controversy made him one of the most beloved and influential figures of Scottish Reformed history. Boston pastored quiet country parishes — Simprin and then Ettrick — for his whole ministry, far from the centers of power, yet his influence spread through his books. His Human Nature in Its Fourfold State (1720) traced the soul through its four conditions — innocence (as created), nature (as fallen), grace (as redeemed), and glory (as consummated) — and became one of the most widely-read works of practical divinity in Scotland for over a century. Boston was a central figure in the Marrow Controversy (1718-1723): he rediscovered and championed the 17th-century English work The Marrow of Modern Divinity, which defended the free offer of the gospel and the distinction between law and grace against a creeping legalism (neonomianism) in the Scottish Kirk. The General Assembly condemned the Marrow; Boston and the "Marrow Men" (including the Erskine brothers) defended it, contending that the gospel offers Christ freely to all sinners as sinners, without prior qualification. Boston also labored in Hebrew studies and wrote a moving spiritual autobiography (Memoirs) that records his afflictions, his buried children, and his persevering faith. He represents the warm, free-grace, experiential heart of Scottish Calvinism.

corruption_summary: Thomas Boston is corrupted when the Marrow's free offer is misread as antinomianism, when his fourfold-state framework is reduced to a quaint scheme, or when the free-grace heart of his preaching is lost to either the legalism he opposed or the license he equally rejected.
corruption_paragraphs: Antinomian misreading of the Marrow. Boston's opponents charged that the Marrow's free offer of Christ to sinners as sinners, without prior qualification, opened the door to antinomianism — cheap grace that ignored the law. The Marrow Men answered carefully: the gospel offers Christ freely (against legalism), AND the law remains the believer's rule of life (against antinomianism). The Marrow distinguished the law as a covenant of works (from which the believer is freed) from the law as a rule of gratitude (to which the believer is bound). Boston held free grace and holy obedience together, refusing both the legalist's qualification of the offer and the antinomian's dismissal of the law.

Scheme-reduction of the fourfold state. Human Nature in Its Fourfold State is sometimes remembered as a tidy four-part outline — innocence, nature, grace, glory — as though it were a mere structural device. Boston's work is a searching, experiential anatomy of the human condition under God: the original righteousness lost in Adam, the total depravity of fallen nature, the renewal of grace in regeneration, and the consummation of glory. It traces the actual spiritual experience of fall and redemption, applied to the conscience with Scottish-Puritan realism. The scheme is the skeleton; the experiential flesh is the point.

etymology: Named for The Marrow of Modern Divinity, a 1645 English work (by "E.F.," likely Edward Fisher) that became the storm-center of a doctrinal controversy in the Church of Scotland from 1718 to 1723.
biblical_def: The Marrow Controversy (1718-1723) was a doctrinal dispute in the Church of Scotland over the free offer of the gospel, the relationship of law and grace, and the danger of legalism (neonomianism) — sparked by the republication of the 1645 English work The Marrow of Modern Divinity. The controversy began when Thomas Boston commended the long-forgotten Marrow to others, and a new Scottish edition (1718) circulated widely. The book taught the free, unconditional offer of Christ to all sinners as sinners, the distinction between the law as a covenant of works and the law as a rule of life, and the believer's freedom from the law's condemning and covenantal power while remaining bound to it as a rule of gratitude. The General Assembly of 1720 condemned the Marrow, charging it with antinomianism and with teaching universal atonement and a kind of cheap grace. Twelve ministers — the "Marrow Men," including Thomas Boston and the brothers Ebenezer and Ralph Erskine — formally protested, arguing that the Assembly had, in its zeal against antinomianism, fallen into the opposite error of legalism: making the gospel offer conditional on the sinner's prior repentance or qualification, rather than free to sinners as sinners. The Assembly rebuked the Marrow Men but did not depose them. The controversy crystallized the Reformed doctrine of the free offer of the gospel: Christ is offered freely and unconditionally to all who hear, the warrant to believe is the gospel command and promise (not the sinner's secret election or prior worthiness), and this free offer is held together with both definite atonement and the abiding rule of the moral law. The Marrow Controversy remains a touchstone in Reformed discussions of the free offer, law and gospel, and the avoidance of both legalism and antinomianism.
webster_summary: A doctrinal dispute in the Church of Scotland (1718-1723) over the free offer of the gospel and the law-grace relationship, sparked by The Marrow of Modern Divinity; the Marrow Men (Boston, the Erskines) defended the free, unconditional offer against the Assembly's legalism.

corruption_summary: The Marrow Controversy is corrupted when reduced to obscure Scottish church politics, when the free offer it defended is collapsed into either Arminian universalism or hyper-Calvinist denial, or when the law-grace balance it secured is lost to either legalism or antinomianism.
corruption_paragraphs: Obscure-politics dismissal. To modern eyes the Marrow Controversy can look like an arcane 18th-century Scottish church squabble. Its doctrinal stakes are perennial: how the gospel is offered to sinners (freely and unconditionally, or only after they qualify themselves), and how law and grace relate in the Christian life. Every generation faces the twin dangers the Marrow named — the legalism that hedges the offer with conditions, and the antinomianism that dismisses the law. The controversy is a permanent reference point precisely because its questions never go away.

Collapsing the free offer. The Marrow's free offer is easily misread in two opposite directions. Arminians hear "Christ offered freely to all" and conclude universal atonement and resistible grace; hyper-Calvinists hear "definite atonement" and conclude the offer cannot be universal. The Marrow Men held the precise Reformed position both miss: the atonement is definite (Christ died effectually for the elect), AND the offer is universal and unconditional (Christ is freely offered to all who hear, and all are warranted and commanded to believe). The warrant to believe is the gospel itself, not the sinner's knowledge of his election. This is the narrow Reformed road between the two errors.

etymology: Named for the Savoy Palace in London, where a synod of Congregational (Independent) churches met in 1658 to adopt the declaration. It is a revision of the Westminster Confession of Faith adapted for Congregational church government.
biblical_def: The Savoy Declaration (1658) is the confession of faith of the English Congregational (Independent) churches — a revision of the Westminster Confession of Faith adapting it to Congregational rather than Presbyterian church government. When the Congregationalists of the Cromwellian era met at the Savoy Palace in London in 1658, under the leadership of theologians including John Owen and Thomas Goodwin, they produced a confession that followed Westminster almost word-for-word in its doctrine while modifying the chapters on church government to reflect their Independent (congregational) polity, in which each local church is self-governing under Christ rather than subject to presbyteries and synods. The Savoy Declaration also strengthened and clarified a few doctrinal points, including a fuller statement on the covenant of grace and on the church. Its historical significance for Baptists is direct: when the Particular Baptists came to write their own confession (the 1677/1689 Second London Baptist Confession), they followed the Savoy Declaration's wording at several points where it had already adapted Westminster for non-Presbyterian, congregational churches — so that the 1689 stands in a line of descent from Westminster (1646) through Savoy (1658) to the Baptists (1677/1689). The three confessions together demonstrate the substantial doctrinal unity of the Reformed tradition across Presbyterian, Congregational, and Baptist church government: they agree almost entirely on the doctrines of God, salvation, and the Christian life, differing chiefly on baptism and the structure of the church.
webster_summary: The 1658 confession of the English Congregational churches; a revision of the Westminster Confession adapted for Congregational government, led by John Owen and Thomas Goodwin; the textual bridge between Westminster (1646) and the Baptist 1689 Confession.

corruption_summary: The Savoy Declaration is corrupted when treated as a minor footnote to Westminster, when the Congregational polity it codified is dismissed as schism, or when its role in the descent of the Baptist 1689 Confession is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: Footnote dismissal. The Savoy Declaration is sometimes treated as a mere derivative of Westminster, barely worth notice. Its significance is real: it is the confessional charter of English Congregationalism, the work of the greatest Congregational theologians of the age (Owen, Goodwin), and the textual bridge by which Westminster's doctrine passed to the Baptists. To understand the 1689 Confession, one must understand that it followed not only Westminster but Savoy — the Congregationalists had already done much of the work of adapting Reformed doctrine for non-Presbyterian, self-governing churches.

Polity-as-schism misreading. Presbyterian critics have sometimes read Congregational (and Baptist) polity as schismatic fragmentation — the breakdown of the church's proper connectional unity. The Congregationalists held their polity as a conviction drawn from Scripture: that Christ governs each local church directly as its head (Col 1:18), through elders the congregation recognizes (Acts 14:23), with the gathered church as the seat of discipline (Matt 18:17). The Savoy Declaration is the careful confessional statement of that conviction. The substantial doctrinal agreement of Westminster, Savoy, and the 1689 shows that the differences over polity, real as they are, sit within a shared Reformed faith.

etymology: The First London Baptist Confession of Faith (1644, revised 1646) was issued by seven Particular Baptist congregations in London. It is "first" in distinction from the later Second London Baptist Confession (1677/1689).
biblical_def: The First London Baptist Confession of Faith (1644, revised 1646) was the earliest confession of the Particular (Calvinistic) Baptists — issued by seven London congregations to demonstrate their Reformed orthodoxy and to distinguish themselves from the continental Anabaptists with whom they were being slanderously confused. In the turbulent years of the English Civil War, the young Particular Baptist movement faced grave suspicion: to practice believer's baptism and to gather churches outside the established order looked, to their enemies, like the radical Anabaptism associated with the disastrous Münster rebellion of the previous century. The seven churches issued the 1644 Confession (signed by figures including William Kiffin and others) precisely to answer the slander: to show that they were sober, orthodox, Calvinistic Christians who held the doctrines of grace, honored the civil magistrate, and differed from the wider Reformed world only on baptism and church government. The First London Confession affirms the Trinity, the sovereignty of God, election, particular redemption, justification by faith, and believer's baptism by immersion (it is among the first confessions to specify immersion as the mode). It is warmer and more compact than the later 1689, and bears the marks of a persecuted minority pleading its orthodoxy. The 1644/1646 Confession established the Particular Baptists as a confessional, Reformed people from their first decade, decisively refuting the later myth that Calvinistic Baptists were a recent innovation upon an originally Arminian or non-confessional Baptist movement. It was succeeded, a generation later, by the fuller Second London Confession (1677/1689).
webster_summary: The earliest Particular Baptist confession (1644, revised 1646), issued by seven London congregations to demonstrate Reformed orthodoxy and distinguish themselves from continental Anabaptism; affirms the doctrines of grace and believer's baptism by immersion.

corruption_summary: The First London Confession is corrupted when forgotten in favor of the more famous 1689, when its anti-Anabaptist purpose is misread as anti-Baptist, or when its existence is ignored by those who claim that Calvinistic Baptists are a recent novelty.
corruption_paragraphs: Confessional-novelty myth. A persistent myth holds that Calvinistic (Reformed) Baptists are a recent development — that the original Baptists were Arminian, non-confessional, or both, and that Reformed Baptists imported their Calvinism later. The 1644 First London Confession is the decisive refutation: in their very first decade, the Particular Baptists issued a fully Calvinistic, confessional statement of faith. The Reformed Baptist tradition is not a recent graft upon an Arminian root; it is the original Particular Baptist stock, confessing the doctrines of grace from the 1640s. The novelty is the amnesia, not the Calvinism.

Anti-Anabaptist purpose misread. The First London Confession was written, in part, to distance the Particular Baptists from the continental Anabaptists — the radical reformers associated with the violent Münster episode and with various heterodox positions. Some modern readers, hearing "Baptist," assume continuity with the Anabaptists and read the 1644 Confession's careful distancing as confusing. The Particular Baptists were emphatic: they were Reformed Christians who practiced believer's baptism, NOT Anabaptist radicals. They honored the magistrate, held orthodox Trinitarian and Christological doctrine, and confessed the Reformed faith. The confession's purpose was to make exactly this distinction clear.

etymology: One of the catechisms produced by the Westminster Assembly (1643-1652). "Larger" distinguishes it from the Westminster Shorter Catechism; both accompany the Westminster Confession of Faith.
biblical_def: The Westminster Larger Catechism (1647) is the fuller of the two catechisms produced by the Westminster Assembly, designed for the public exposition of Christian doctrine and for the instruction of those advanced in the faith, while its companion the Shorter Catechism served for the beginner and the child. Together with the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Shorter Catechism, it forms the Westminster Standards, the doctrinal foundation of English-speaking Presbyterianism. Consisting of 196 questions and answers, the Larger Catechism follows the same structure as the Shorter — what man is to believe concerning God, and what duty God requires of man — but in far greater detail. It contains the most extensive confessional exposition of the Ten Commandments in the Reformed tradition, drawing out from each commandment its required duties and forbidden sins with searching thoroughness (so that the seventh commandment, for instance, is shown to forbid not only adultery but every impurity of thought, word, look, and deed). Its treatment of the office and work of Christ, of the sacraments, of the church, and of the means of grace is correspondingly full. While the Shorter Catechism became the universal instrument of basic instruction, the Larger Catechism served preachers, teachers, and serious students as a comprehensive doctrinal and ethical reference. Its exposition of the moral law in particular has shaped Reformed ethics for nearly four centuries, and it remains a subordinate standard in confessional Presbyterian churches and a treasured resource across the broader Reformed world.
webster_summary: The fuller of the two Westminster catechisms (1647), 196 questions for advanced instruction and public exposition; contains the most extensive Reformed confessional treatment of the Ten Commandments; part of the Westminster Standards with the Confession and Shorter Catechism.

corruption_summary: The Westminster Larger Catechism is corrupted when its thorough exposition of the law is dismissed as legalism, when it is neglected in favor of the Shorter Catechism alone, or when its searching application of the commandments to thought and motive is softened to accommodate the modern conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: Law-as-legalism misreading. The Larger Catechism's exhaustive exposition of the Ten Commandments — drawing from each commandment a wide range of required duties and forbidden sins, reaching to the thoughts and motives of the heart — can be mistaken for legalism, as though it bound the conscience to an oppressive code. The Reformed reading is the opposite: the law searched in this depth drives the sinner to Christ (the law's pedagogical use, Gal 3:24), and serves the believer as the rule of grateful obedience (the law's third use). The Catechism expounds the law so thoroughly precisely to show that no one can be justified by it, and to direct the justified believer in the path of holiness. The thoroughness serves the gospel.

Neglect for the Shorter alone. Most who know the Westminster catechisms know only the Shorter — rightly beloved for its compact, memorizable answers. The Larger Catechism, longer and less often memorized, is correspondingly neglected. Yet it contains treasures the Shorter only summarizes: the fullest Reformed treatment of the moral law, extended expositions of Christ's offices and the means of grace, and searching ethical application. The serious student of Reformed theology who stops at the Shorter has tasted only the introduction; the Larger Catechism is the fuller meal.
